The rest of the batch was checked, and the document validated, without the failed ops applied, so an error listed after it may only follow from an earlier one and go away once that is fixed, and an op that passed here may still fail then.

ops[5]: person_evidence for 'I2' (assertion 'a_017') records match_score 0.78 with no same_person score behind it. Call same_person({ projectPath, assertionId: 'a_017', treePersonId: 'I2' }) first, then write the link with the score it returns. The tool assembles both sides itself, so this costs one call and no payload. I1's tree attests birth ~1859. Both records attest birth ~1854 (Great Register: age 21 in 1875 → ~1854; passenger index: stated 1854). quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

review_dimensions.name: Confidence calibration

The rule is properly applied: the strong name, age, and household correlation across two independent censuses would normally support 'confident', but the unexplained transatlantic move (Sussex to Tennessee, 6804 km, no passenger list or naturalization record in project, no corridor on wiki page) caps it at 'probable'. The rationales explicitly name the geographic gap and the absence of a documentary bridge, meeting the decided rule requirement. No links are incorrectly marked 'confident' or over-applied as 'speculative'.

dimensions.name: Correctness

Confidence levels are correctly calibrated to 'probable' across all links, reflecting the unexplained transatlantic move. The rationales accurately cite the geographic gap (6804 km, no documentary bridge, no corridor on the Tennessee wiki page). Residence facts were materialized correctly to the tree. No fabricated material or unsupported claims.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: All 20 assertions from both census records (src_001 and src_002) were linked to appropriate tree persons. Both the 1870 household (5 persons, 11 assertions) and 1880 household (3 persons, 9 assertions) were fully processed. Relationship assertions (wife-of, son-of) were linked to both parties as required. The skill identified and flagged the absence of James and Ellen from the 1880 census as worth investigating, demonstrating thorough coverage.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed correct arguments. same_person calls correctly paired assertions with tree persons (a_001→I1, a_003→I2, etc.). place_search and place_distance were called with correct place names ('Maury County, Tennessee' and 'Horsham, Sussex, England'). wiki_read correctly targeted Tennessee_Emigration_and_Immigration. materialize_facts calls correctly specified personId, recordId, and recordRole for each household member. research_append calls properly formatted person_evidence entries with all required fields.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All 22 person_evidence entries correctly use 'probable' confidence. The rule is properly applied: the strong name, age, and household correlation across two independent censuses would normally support 'confident', but the unexplained transatlantic move (Sussex to Tennessee, 6804 km, no passenger list or naturalization record in project, no corridor on wiki page) caps it at 'probable'. The rationales explicitly name the geographic gap and the absence of a documentary bridge, meeting the decided rule requirement. No links are incorrectly marked 'confident' or over-applied as 'speculative'.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Rationales cite specific matching attributes: exact name matches ('William Weller', 'Mary Weller', etc.), consistent birth years (~1825, ~1828, ~1852, ~1855, ~1859), England birthplaces, household positions (head, wife, son, household_member_2/3/4), and age progression across censuses (e.g., 'age 45 in 1870, age 55 in 1880'). They address the geographic gap explicitly: 'Maury County, Tennessee, 1870 vs nearest attested residence Horsham, Sussex, England (pre-run): outside 6804 km. Tennessee emigration wiki page names no arrival corridor from England in this era; no documentary bridge (passenger list, naturalization) found in the project.' Disambiguation is implicit in the household structure and relationship positions.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
dimensions.rationale: Relationship assertions in the 1880 census (a_019 wife-of-William, a_020 son-of-William) are linked to both parties. a_019 generates pe_019 (I2) and pe_020 (I1); a_020 generates pe_021 (I5) and pe_022 (I1). Each relationship is represented from both sides, satisfying the cardinality requirement. The head (I1) is correctly included in relationship links via recordRole specification in same_person calls.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: No new persons required minting; all five household members (I1, I2, I3, I4, I5) already existed in the tree. materialize_facts was correctly invoked for both censuses to enrich existing persons with sourced facts (birth years, residence facts). The 1870 census enriched all five persons; the 1880 census enriched I1, I2, I5 (James and Ellen absent from 1880). No new edges were written because the household skeleton (couple R1, parent-child R2–R7) already existed. This is correct: edges are owed only when a household record introduces new relationships, and these relationships pre-existed. The skill correctly did not attempt to create redundant edges.

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every assertion with a tree candidate: a_001, a_003, a_005, a_007, a_009 (1870 census personas CP1–CP5 to I1–I5); a_012, a_014, a_016 (1880 census personas DP1, DP2, DP3 to I1, I2, I5); and relationship assertions a_019, a_020 with recordRole specified for the head party. Each call returned score 0.78 (matched: true), which was recorded in match_score and used to inform—not dictate—the confidence decision. The high score did not override the geographic constraint; confidence remained 'probable' despite the strong correlation, correctly applying the rule that a qualitative conflict (unexplained move) caps confidence regardless of score.
